source.title: Safety Measurements for Fine-tuned LLMs Should be Grounded in Capability
source.authors: Krishnapriya Vishnubhotla; Hillary Dawkins; Isar Nejadgholi; S. Kiritchenko

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. No apparent truncation or wrong-document issue.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests benign supervised fine-tuning and reports that safety outcomes vary by model, dataset, benchmark, and evaluator; some settings degrade measured safety while others improve it.
record.gate_note: Own results bear on V2 through harmfulness and compliance measurements after benign fine-tuning. The forced-choice bypass statement in the discussion cites another study and is not an own result. The paper does not measure harmful fine-tuning on small datasets, per-token KL, compliant-prefix or suffix attacks, decoding changes, safety-localized weights, or token-depth training.
record.test_reason: The study's own LoRA fine-tuning results on benign data (GSM8k, Science10k, ARC, BoolQ, Alpaca15k) report harmfulness and compliance rates against the instruction-tuned base for four models. It argues V2's erosion is not uniform: it depends on model, dataset, checkpoint, benchmark and evaluator, and often reverses.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that benign fine-tuning can degrade or improve safety relative to the base depending on benchmark and evaluator. Safety tends to degrade early and recover with more epochs, by mechanisms that are unclear. Constrained-output fine-tuning causes incoherent outputs that automated judges misread. Safety measurement should therefore be grounded in capability and coherence. SafeLoRA shows variable safety-capability trade-offs.
record.recipe_differences: Benign supervised LoRA fine-tuning on task datasets, including thousands of examples, rather than harmful-example fine-tuning. Evaluates harmfulness/refusal over 1,840 safety prompts with LlamaGuard-8B and a SORRY-Bench evaluator; also varies models, datasets, epochs, and benchmark subsets.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with model, fine-tuning dataset, epoch/checkpoint selection, LoRA configuration, safety benchmark, evaluator, and output coherence. Constrained output datasets ARC and BoolQ can produce incoherent safety-prompt responses and unreliable LlamaGuard judgments.

fits_no_version.finding: SafeLoRA safety-subspace projection mostly lowers harmfulness, but costs up to ~10 points of accuracy on Llama Science10k and degrades safety for Qwen-8B Science10k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-subspace projection mitigations trade capability for safety, and do so inconsistently across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Constrained-format fine-tuning yields incoherent replies to safety prompts, which LlamaGuard misjudges as unsafe. Harmfulness rises with perplexity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured benign-fine-tuning safety loss can be an artifact of incoherence plus judge error.

record.problems: The authors state that the tested model families and sizes, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and task datasets are limited; experiments cover only English and supervised LoRA. They identify incoherent outputs and unreliable automated safety judgments for constrained-format fine-tuning. Table 1 gives selected checkpoints, and the text does not state uncertainty for those table values.
record.rows_left_out: No Table 1 harmfulness rows were omitted. Other Figure 1 epoch-by-task trajectories, Figure 3 comparisons across all models, and Figure 4 benchmark traces for Alpaca15k and Science10k were not separately extracted where the text provides no condition-specific outcome beyond the displayed figures; relevant explicit aggregate statements and the stated GSM8k benchmark contrast are included.

untested.parts: Not tested: the few-to-hundreds benign-example regime, carefully selected safety-breaking benign data, full-parameter fine-tuning, and larger or closed models. Only LoRA on thousands of examples, models of 1-8B.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks. The MCQ bypass is cited from other work.
SafeLoRA uses a safety subspace, but localization is not tested.
No test of causes of shallowness.

missing.what: Across models, harmfulness rises in epochs 1-2 and then recovers toward later epochs. This is an early-checkpoint erosion pattern, not captured as its own row.

Alpaca15k (the classic Qi et al. benign dataset) harmfulness and compliance trajectories for all four models. Only Llama-1B is rowed (R55). Text says compliance exceeds harmfulness and the two correlate more with model size.
Llama-8B Alpaca15k and Science10k harmfulness by benchmark subset.

record.verdict_notes: The record's first supports label wrongly names Qwen-8B for the BeaverTails-Intent GSM8k result; it is Llama-8B (R54). SafeLoRA rows are re-linked to none because they evaluate a mitigation, and SafeLoRA-safe values are chosen for lowest harmfulness. Qwen-4B's base harmfulness (27%) is unusually high, so its improvement may partly reflect regression from a poor start. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning dataset or harmful-example count is tested.
Tests benign supervised LoRA on Alpaca15k, GSM8k, Science10k, ARC, and BoolQ; does not test carefully selected safety-breaking benign examples or a few-to-a-few-hundred-example regime.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding-change experiments. The discussion's forced-choice bypass reference is to other work.
No experiment localizes safety behavior to a small set of weights or ranks.
The paper does not test whether the data or training objective causes token-level shallowness.
SafeLoRA is evaluated as a fine-tuning mitigation, not as a method for spreading safety beyond early response tokens; robustness of token-depth safety is not tested.
